closing_note.summary:
Clinical problem: A 28-year-old man presents with 5 days of polyuria, polydipsia, dry mouth, and 19 kg weight loss over ~16 weeks (94 to 75 kg). He used tirzepatide without supervision for weight loss (escalating to 7.5 mg weekly, then intermittent 5 mg), stopping 4 weeks before symptom onset. No prior diabetes diagnosis; previous fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L (2 years ago) and fingerstick 5.8 mmol/L pre-treatment. Admission fasting glucose 13.99 mmol/L, HbA1c 10.8%, confirming significant chronic hyperglycemia.

Prioritised explanations:
1. New-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus: Strongest fit. Age, marked weight loss, severe hyperglycemia with HbA1c 10.8% indicating weeks-months of dysglycemia. Tirzepatide may have partially masked hyperglycemia during use; cessation unmasked symptomatic decompensation.
2. Type 1 diabetes: Possible but less likely without ketosis data. Weight loss and age compatible; requires autoantibody/C-peptide testing.
3. Medication-related hyperglycemia: Tirzepatide withdrawal may precipitate hyperglycemia in susceptible individuals, but HbA1c 10.8% suggests hyperglycemia predated or persisted during treatment. History cannot establish whether tirzepatide induced beta-cell stress or simply treated undiagnosed diabetes.

Metabolic risk: High. Symptomatic hyperglycemia with HbA1c 10.8% risks diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state. Urgent ketone, venous gas, electrolyte, and renal assessment needed.

Next actions: Exclude DKA/HHS (ketones, blood gas, electrolytes, renal function). Measure C-peptide and islet autoantibodies to clarify subtype. Initiate insulin therapy per acute hyperglycemia guidelines. Arrange diabetes education and specialist follow-up.

Clinical problem: 28‑year‑old man with five days of polyuria, polydipsia, dry mouth and a 19 kg weight loss (94 kg to 75 kg) over approximately 16 weeks. Admission fasting glucose 13.99 mmol/L and HbA1c 10.8 % indicate marked hyperglycaemia and high metabolic risk for diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar state.

Prioritised explanations:
1. New‑onset diabetes mellitus (type 1 or type 2) – supported by severe hyperglycaemia, elevated HbA1c, classic osmotic symptoms; uncertainty: subtype not yet defined, need autoantibodies and C‑peptide.
2. Diabetes insipidus – would produce polyuria with normal glucose; unlikely given glucose 13.99 mmol/L, but not excluded without water‑deprivation test.
3. Medication‑related effect of unsupervised tirzepatide – patient used weekly doses up to 7.5 mg for weight loss; symptoms began four weeks after last dose. Tirzepatide can improve glycaemia, but withdrawal may unmask latent diabetes; however, no prior diabetes diagnosis and prior fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L two years ago. Causality cannot be confirmed without pancreatic function data.

Next steps: obtain venous blood gas, ketones, electrolytes, renal function, and calculate anion gap; check for ketonaemia to assess DKA risk; order autoantibodies (GAD, IA‑2) and C‑peptide; repeat glucose monitoring; evaluate fluid status and initiate insulin therapy per protocol; document tirzepatide timeline for pharmacovigilance.
